name: libev
workload: bench.c from libev's comparison (derived from libevent's bench.c), run as bench-libev vs bench-libevent with -n 100000 -r 10: 100,000 pipes registered with the event loop, one active client, measuring microseconds for the whole iteration (re-registering every watcher plus dispatch) and for the dispatch phase alone.
claimed_speedup: Total time per iteration, runs 2-10 of 10 in the README listing: libev 27,356-28,284 us vs libevent 117,167-129,374 us, about 4.5x faster (means 27,683 vs 123,354 us, derived from page data); the dispatch-only column goes the other way (libev 264-340 us vs libevent 213-224 us, libevent about 1.29x faster, derived from page data). The README concludes 'on my system libev performed best, with close second being picoev'.
compiler_and_flags: bench programs built with CC -Os -ggdb (Makefile CCFLAGS); how the libev and libevent submodules are built is not stated
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars on the enki/libev GitHub mirror; packaged by Debian and Homebrew; the Perl EV module bundles it
tradeoffs: Lower-level API than libevent or libuv (explicit watcher structs, no bundled cross-platform abstraction beyond POSIX backends, weaker Windows support); the libevent compatibility layer emulates only the libevent 1.4.1-beta API and is not ABI compatible.
caveats: Measured here from the third-party repo bartman/event-loop-benchmark (5 stars, 18 commits, January 2018): README says 'on my system' with no CPU, OS or compiler version, flags -Os only for the bench programs, submodule versions not pinned in the README, no licence stated on the repo page. Its two unlabelled columns were read from bench.c (first = setup plus dispatch from gettimeofday ta, second = dispatch loop only from ts). The libev author's own page http://libev.schmorp.de/bench.html (libevent 1.4.3 vs libev 3.31) is the primary source: per search-result excerpts it uses gcc 4.2.3 with -O3 -fno-guess-branch-probability -g on a Core2 Quad at 3.6GHz, Debian kernel 2.6.24-1, says libevent takes almost twice as much time per iteration without timeouts and that with idle timeouts libev is faster by a factor of two to almost three, and links the public bench.c; that page was EGRESS_BLOCKED in this session so those numbers are snippet only (wave 5 already holds a tier A libev record from event-loops-shootouts built on that page, so this record should fold into it). Both benchmark sources are old and first-party or hobbyist; a forum post (bbs.archlinux.org thread 90783, date not seen, blocked here, search excerpt only) reports libevent 2.0.3-alpha finishing 100 to 150 microseconds quicker than libev 3.9 with bench.c, disputed in the thread as possibly measuring libevent against itself.

name: libevent
workload: bench.c from libev's comparison, run as bench-libevent vs bench-libuv with -n 100000 -r 10: 100,000 pipes registered with the event loop, one active client, microseconds per iteration (re-registration plus dispatch) and for the dispatch phase alone.
claimed_speedup: Total time per iteration, runs 2-10 of 10: libevent 117,167-129,374 us vs libuv 163,320-171,014 us, about 1.36x faster (means 123,354 vs 167,733 us, derived from page data); libuev 150,834-157,453 us. Dispatch-only column: libevent 213-224 us vs libuv 80,036-84,936 us (about 380x, derived from page data, implausibly large). libev is faster than libevent on the total column (27,356-28,284 us) while libevent beats libev on the dispatch column (213-224 us vs 264-340 us, about 1.29x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: bench programs built with CC -Os -ggdb (Makefile CCFLAGS); how the libevent and libuv submodules are built is not stated
tradeoffs: Callback-based C API with evbuffer/bufferevent layers, optional OpenSSL, built-in evhttp/evdns; heavier than libev or picoev on setup cost (4.5x slower than libev on the total column here); libuv offers a larger platform abstraction (filesystem, processes, Windows IOCP).
caveats: Numbers come from one third-party hobbyist repo (bartman/event-loop-benchmark, 5 stars, 18 commits in January 2018): README says 'on my system', no CPU, OS or compiler version; -Os only for the bench programs; submodule revisions not stated; columns unlabelled (read from bench.c as setup plus dispatch, and dispatch only). The libuv harness uses uv_run(UV_RUN_ONCE) in a loop while libev uses EVRUN_NOWAIT and libevent EVLOOP_NONBLOCK, and the 380x dispatch ratio looks like a harness artifact, so tier is capped at C. The README's own conclusion is that libev wins and picoev is second; libevent is not the winner. No libevent project page, README or whatsnew file carries a baseline comparison; whatsnew-2.0/2.1/2.2.txt mention speedups only against earlier internal behaviour. Niels Provos' 'Small Libevent 2.0 Performance Test' (provos.org, blocked here, search excerpt only) reports evhttp 1450.79 req/s on libevent 1.4.10, 1961.99 on 2.0 and 3979.31 on 2.0 with evbuffer_add_reference (ab, 15,000 requests, 40 parallel, 200,000-byte body), which is version-over-version rather than against another library.

name: libidn
workload: Ruby benchmark/idna.rb in a pull request to the addressable gem: 100,000 cycles of converting the single domain string 'fiᆵリ宠퐱卄.com' to ASCII ('xn--fi-w1k207vk59a3qk9w9r.com') and back, through the pure Ruby IDNA code, the libidn (v1) backend and a new libidn2 FFI backend.
claimed_speedup: Ruby Benchmark rehearsal output, real time for 100,000 cycles: pure Ruby 5.915326 s, libidn 0.522676 s, libidn2 0.763983 s; libidn about 1.46x faster than libidn2 and about 11.3x faster than pure Ruby (both derived from page data). The PR author calls libidn2 'slower than libidn1' but above 100k iterations/sec.
stars_or_usage: GNU library shipped by Linux distributions; stars not shown on the GitLab mirror page
tradeoffs: Implements IDNA2003 (stringprep, nameprep, punycode, TLD checks) which is obsolete for browsers and registries; libidn2 implements IDNA2008 with UTS #46 compatibility processing and does more work per name, so the speed gap partly reflects fewer checks. Library files are dual LGPL-3.0-or-later or GPL-2.0-or-later (tools GPL-3.0-or-later).
caveats: One input string, wall time through Ruby FFI/binding layers rather than raw C calls, no hardware, Ruby version or compiler stated, and the PR (March 2023, author jarthod) is still open and unmerged. The libidn1 vs libidn2 gap is an incidental side result of a wrapper benchmark, not a claim by the libidn project, whose README and NEWS make no performance claim. libidn2's own merge request 134 ('punycode decode: slightly faster for common cases', up to 5 percent) compares libidn2 against itself.
